paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent needs to earn rewards while remaining reliable when its inputs are disturbed. Randomized smoothing is one technique for improving robustness, but existing smoothed agents can perform poorly even without attacks. This paper addresses both sides of that problem: maintaining useful behavior in clean conditions and resisting adversarial interference.

The authors introduce two training approaches, S-DQN and S-PPO, for producing more effective smoothed agents. Across standard reinforcement learning benchmarks, they report improvements in clean rewards, measured resistance to attacks, and robustness guarantees. These are distinct outcomes: performance under tested attacks provides empirical evidence, while a robustness guarantee supplies a theoretical form of assurance.

Under the strongest attack in their evaluation, the agents outperform existing smoothed agents by an average factor of 2.16 and previous robustly trained agents by 2.13. The paper also introduces Smoothed Attack, reported to be 1.89 times more effective at reducing smoothed agents’ rewards than existing attacks. Together, the contributions improve both agent training and the evaluation of smoothed agents’ vulnerabilities.
icml-2024-breaking-the-barrier-enhanced-.tldr: S-DQN and S-PPO improve smoothed reinforcement learning agents’ rewards and robustness, while a new attack strengthens their evaluation.

paragraphs: Randomized experiments become more complicated when several treatment administrators compete for the same people’s attention. A participant’s response can depend on where a treatment appears, so competition changes the effect being measured. The paper studies this interaction in settings such as field experiments and online advertising, where access to subjects is itself strategically contested.

The authors build a game in which agents bid for subjects and seek to reduce error in their causal estimates. Their central technical step replaces the difficult estimation objective with a tractable approximation. This alternative objective measures the value of samples obtained by strategically allocating a budget across subjects, connecting spending decisions to the quality of experimental evidence.

For the tractable objective, the authors establish the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium: a stable combination of strategies where no agent benefits from changing alone. Under broad conditions, any Nash equilibrium also approximately satisfies the original estimation objective’s equilibrium requirement. The result explains how competing experimenters can reach stable behavior while pursuing informative data, with the connection to estimation error remaining approximate and conditional.
icml-2024-causal-inference-from-competin.tldr: A game-theoretic model connects competing experimenters’ budget decisions to causal estimation error through a tractable equilibrium approximation.

paragraphs: An image contains multiple factors that jointly determine its appearance, including objects, shadows, and broader scene characteristics. Being able to separate those factors would make it possible to reuse parts of one scene in another. This paper develops Decomp Diffusion, an unsupervised method that infers a collection of components from a single input image.

Each inferred component is represented by a diffusion model. This gives the decomposition a generative role: the components are usable ingredients for producing images. The demonstrated factors operate at different scales, including local content such as individual objects and broader characteristics such as shadows or facial expressions. The method therefore goes beyond treating every component as a separate spatial object.

The authors show that inferred factors can be recombined flexibly, including with factors obtained from other models. These combinations generate scenes substantially different from those encountered during training. The significance is the connection between understanding an image’s constituent factors and controlling new image generation: the same inferred representations support both decomposition and recombination.
icml-2024-compositional-image-decomposit.tldr: Decomp Diffusion separates an image into generative components that can be recombined to create substantially different scenes.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can satisfy its constraints during training and still violate them after deployment. The problem arises when the real environment behaves differently from the training environment. This paper treats that mismatch as a central part of learning, rather than judging a policy only by its performance under the training model.

The authors formulate constrained reinforcement learning under model uncertainty. The objective combines earning rewards with satisfying a constraint despite differences in environment dynamics. They develop Robust Constrained Policy Optimization, or RCPO, to address this formulation in large or continuous state spaces. That scope matters because the method is intended to handle settings beyond small, explicitly enumerated collections of states.

RCPO comes with theoretical guarantees concerning worst-case reward improvement and constraint violation at each training iteration. These guarantees address how learning progresses under the paper’s uncertainty formulation; they should not be read as an unrestricted promise about every deployment environment. Experiments on reinforcement learning tasks with constraints demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution brings model mismatch into both policy optimization and its accompanying theoretical analysis.
icml-2024-constrained-reinforcement-lear.tldr: RCPO learns constrained policies under model uncertainty, with per-iteration guarantees on worst-case reward improvement and constraint violation.

paragraphs: Serving large language models across multiple devices can leave expensive accelerators underused. The paper identifies three sources of inefficiency: prompt processing and token generation have different latency patterns, GPU memory is overprovisioned, and failures can require lengthy recovery. In pipeline-parallel deployments, the processing mismatch creates idle gaps that reduce useful hardware work.

DéjàVu addresses these problems through DéjàVuLib, a library for efficiently streaming the model’s key-value cache. The cache holds state used during generation, making its movement relevant to both execution and recovery. The system uses the library to separate prompt processing from token processing, swap microbatches for memory management, and replicate state for fault tolerance.

Each mechanism targets a different operational cost. Separating processing stages reduces pipeline gaps, swapping helps manage GPU memory efficiently, and replication supports recovery after failures. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of these solutions across a range of large models in cloud deployments. The unifying contribution is a reusable cache-streaming facility that supports several improvements to distributed serving within the same system.
icml-2024-dejavu-kv-cache-streaming-for-.tldr: DéjàVu uses KV-cache streaming to improve distributed LLM utilization, memory management, and recovery from failures.

paragraphs: A decision support system can offer experts a set of possible labels and require them to choose within it. This avoids asking experts to interpret a single imperfect prediction, but it creates a design question: how should the system select the set? Earlier approaches relied on simplified models of expert behavior, making their practical promise uncertain.

The authors develop an online learning methodology that does not require an expert model. It uses the nested structure of conformal prediction sets, where sets can be ordered by inclusion, together with a counterfactual monotonicity assumption. Those ingredients yield an exponential improvement in regret compared with ordinary bandit algorithms. The improvement depends on the stated structural assumption.

A study with 2,751 human participants compares the methodology with several competitive alternatives. Within these prediction-set support systems, limiting experts’ freedom to choose outside the offered set produces better performance than always allowing unrestricted agency. The finding concerns this form of decision support and its evaluation, while the methodological contribution shows how to adapt support without specifying a behavioral model of the expert.
icml-2024-designing-decision-support-sys.tldr: An online method learns prediction-set support without an expert model, and a human study finds benefits from restricting choices to those sets.

paragraphs: Data can occupy a lower-dimensional shape within a much larger space of possible observations. Its intrinsic dimension describes the dimension of that underlying shape, or manifold. This paper shows how a trained diffusion model contains information about that geometry and uses the connection to construct an estimator of intrinsic dimension.

The argument starts from the score function, which describes the direction in which the log probability density increases fastest. Diffusion models approximate this function for data corrupted by different amounts of noise. The authors prove that, as corruption decreases, the score points toward the data manifold. At low noise levels, this supplies an approximation to the manifold’s normal bundle: the collection of directions perpendicular to it.

Knowing these normal directions allows the method to estimate the dimension of the manifold itself. The contribution therefore turns a learned generative model into a tool for measuring data geometry. In controlled experiments involving Euclidean and image data, the proposed estimator outperforms established alternatives. The theoretical connection explains the estimator’s basis, while those experiments support its practical effectiveness in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-diffusion-models-encode-the-in.tldr: The paper proves a connection between diffusion scores and manifold geometry, then uses it to estimate data’s intrinsic dimension.

paragraphs: Generating discrete sequences through diffusion or flow models could offer speed and control advantages over generating one symbol at a time. This paper identifies a problem with a straightforward approach: linear flow matching on the simplex, the space of categorical probability vectors, creates discontinuous training targets and other pathologies.

The authors replace those linear paths with probability paths built from mixtures of Dirichlet distributions. They derive a relationship between the mixtures’ scores and the flow’s vector field, enabling both classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance. These mechanisms let generation respond to desired properties. A distilled version compresses generation into one step, with minimal reported performance loss and speedups that scale as O(L) relative to autoregressive generation for sequence length L.

On complex DNA generation tasks, the method surpasses all evaluated baselines in distributional metrics and in meeting requested design targets. The authors also find that their classifier-free guidance improves unconditional generation and helps produce DNA satisfying specified targets. The results connect the mathematical redesign of the flow paths to faster sampling and stronger control in the evaluated sequence-design tasks.
icml-2024-dirichlet-flow-matching-with-a.tldr: Dirichlet flow matching enables guided DNA sequence generation and one-step sampling with minimal reported performance loss.

paragraphs: Emergency department diagnosis often involves triage followed by multiple laboratory tests, creating delays that contribute to crowding. This paper studies diagnostic assistance that considers both predictive accuracy and time cost. Working with clinicians, the authors curate MIMIC-ED-Assist from public patient data to evaluate test recommendations and predictions of critical outcomes, including death.

Their system, ED-Copilot, recommends patient-specific laboratory tests sequentially while making diagnostic predictions. A pretrained biomedical language model encodes patient information, and reinforcement learning balances reducing wait time against improving prediction accuracy. On the benchmark, ED-Copilot improves accuracy over baselines while reducing average wait time from four hours to two. The authors also report recommendations that adapt to patient severity.

These findings come from a retrospective benchmark, whose recorded histories restrict the system to recommending observed tests. That restriction is part of interpreting the reported gains. The authors additionally show competitive performance when the restriction is removed as the maximum allowed time increases. The work demonstrates a benchmark-based approach to coordinating test selection and prediction, with potential as a diagnostic assistant.
icml-2024-ed-copilot-reduce-emergency-de.tldr: On a retrospective emergency-department benchmark, ED-Copilot improves prediction accuracy while halving average wait time through sequential test recommendations.

paragraphs: RNA function and stability depend closely on its secondary structure, the pattern of pairings that gives it a two-dimensional conformation. Predicted structures must obey biological rules, including allowed pairing types and restrictions against sharp bends. Machine learning predictions can violate these rules, and existing post-processing approaches can still leave invalid structures.

The paper introduces a post-processing framework inspired by the assignment problem in integer linear programming. It acts on machine learning predictions to make them satisfy the relevant structural constraints. The central contribution is a theoretical guarantee that the resulting predictions obey fundamental RNA constraints, giving the correction procedure a formal basis beyond empirical success alone.

The authors report improved predictive performance, no constraint violations, and lower running time in their empirical evaluation. These outcomes matter together: a correction method should produce valid structures without sacrificing its usefulness as a predictor or adding excessive computational cost. The work connects a constrained optimization formulation to biological structure prediction, providing a way to enforce structural requirements after an ML model has produced its initial output.
icml-2024-enforcing-constraints-in-rna-s.tldr: An assignment-inspired post-processing method guarantees fundamental RNA constraints while improving prediction performance and runtime in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Video offers linked visual and auditory information, but learning useful audio-visual representations and generating audio from video have often been treated separately. Vision to Audio and Beyond, or VAB, combines these objectives in one framework. The aim is to learn representations that also support producing audio conditioned on visual content.

VAB operates on encoded representations instead of raw frames and audio. A pretrained audio tokenizer supplies audio tokens, while an image encoder supplies visual features. During pretraining, the model predicts masked audio tokens using visual context. This task supports contextual representation learning alongside video-to-audio generation, making a single training setup serve both purposes.

After pretraining, iterative decoding generates audio tokens conditioned on the visual features. The same model backbone can also be fine-tuned for downstream audio-visual tasks. Experiments report efficient production of high-quality audio from video and competitive retrieval and classification results. These findings support the central idea that a shared latent-space model can learn meaningful cross-modal features while retaining the ability to generate one modality from another.
icml-2024-from-vision-to-audio-and-beyon.tldr: VAB unifies video-to-audio generation and audio-visual representation learning through visually conditioned prediction of masked audio tokens.

paragraphs: Algorithmic tasks offer a setting where researchers can try to explain an entire neural computation. This paper studies fully connected networks with one hidden layer that have learned the arithmetic of the permutation groups S5 and S6. These groups describe ways of rearranging five or six elements, providing a structured problem for investigating learned mechanisms.

The authors report completely reverse engineering the networks. Their explanation shows that the models discover genuine subgroup structure and use neural circuits that break down group arithmetic through those subgroups. This connects the networks’ internal computations to mathematical structure in the task, rather than merely describing which inputs produce correct outputs.

The paper also explains how the researchers checked that their proposed mechanism faithfully described the circuits’ functionality. It compares its account with earlier work claiming a different algorithm for the same problem, highlighting challenges in establishing reliable mechanistic explanations. The contribution is therefore both a detailed account of these particular networks and an examination of how competing interpretations of learned computation should be assessed.
icml-2024-grokking-group-multiplication-.tldr: The authors reverse engineer small networks performing permutation-group arithmetic and find circuits organized around genuine subgroup structure.

paragraphs: Many protein functions depend on binding small molecules, including the interactions involved in enzymatic catalysis. Designing a binding pocket therefore requires attention to both its molecular composition and the three-dimensional arrangement of the bound molecule. This paper develops connected generative methods for modeling those structures and designing the surrounding protein pocket.

The first method, HarmonicFlow, generates three-dimensional protein–ligand binding structures using a self-conditioned flow-matching objective. The authors then extend this model into FlowSite, which jointly generates the pocket’s discrete residue types and the molecule’s binding geometry. Joint generation brings the choice of pocket composition and the proposed bound structure into the same modeling process.

For pocket-level docking, HarmonicFlow improves on state-of-the-art generative processes in simplicity, generality, and average sample quality, according to the reported evaluation. Using this structure-modeling capability, FlowSite designs binding sites substantially better than the baseline approaches. The contribution links improved docking generation to binding-site design, addressing two connected aspects of creating protein pockets for small molecules.
icml-2024-harmonic-self-conditioned-flow.tldr: HarmonicFlow improves binding-structure generation, and FlowSite extends it to jointly design pocket residues and molecular binding geometry.

paragraphs: In a market with competing services, each provider learns from the users who choose it. Better or different models can change which provider a user selects next, which in turn changes the data available for future learning. This paper formalizes that feedback loop between user choice and incremental model updates.

The authors develop a simple, efficient decentralized algorithm aimed at locally minimizing overall user loss. Its target reflects outcomes across users, while its decentralized structure allows learning to proceed across the competing providers. The formulation treats the evolving allocation of users as part of the learning problem, because the models themselves influence which data each service receives.

The theoretical result establishes that the algorithm converges asymptotically to stationary points of overall loss almost surely. This is a convergence statement about stationary points, rather than a guarantee of reaching a global optimum. Experiments using real-world data also demonstrate the algorithm’s utility. Together, the analysis and evaluation address learning in markets where the stream of training data is shaped by users’ responses to the current services.
icml-2024-learning-from-streaming-data-w.tldr: A decentralized learning algorithm accounts for user-choice feedback and converges almost surely to stationary points of overall user loss.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through interpretable concept representations. Users can correct those concept values to improve an output, but such interventions have typically been used once and then discarded. This paper introduces concept bottleneck memory models, or CB2Ms, so that a correction can remain useful when related situations appear later.

CB2Ms use a two-part memory to identify errors and reuse earlier interventions in appropriate new cases. This allows a model to improve automatically from a small initial collection of human corrections. When no previous interventions exist, the system can instead flag potential concept mistakes and request targeted feedback, helping direct the user’s attention.

Experiments involving distribution shifts and confounded data show that CB2Ms can transfer interventions to unseen examples and identify incorrectly inferred concepts. The stated benefit is a more efficient interaction process: users provide corrections that can inform future predictions, while the model helps select where further correction is needed. The results support reuse in the evaluated challenging settings, with appropriate application to new situations remaining central to the method.
icml-2024-learning-to-intervene-on-conce.tldr: Concept bottleneck memory models retain human corrections, reuse them in suitable new situations, and request targeted feedback when needed.

paragraphs: Link-prediction systems recommend relationships such as collaborators, friends, or relevant academic connections. Their predictions can affect who gains further connections and influence. This paper examines inequality within social groups, focusing on whether already well-connected members receive an additional advantage from graph-based prediction.

The authors theoretically show that graph convolutional networks using a symmetrically normalized graph filter exhibit within-group preferential attachment bias. This ties the model’s prediction behavior to existing differences in network degree, or number of connections. They validate the analysis on real-world citation, collaboration, and online social networks, connecting a specific architectural property to the possibility of reinforcing existing network imbalances.

The paper then introduces a fairness metric that measures differences in link-prediction scores among members of the same social group. It also proposes a simple training-time strategy to reduce this unfairness, with demonstrated effectiveness on citation, social, and credit networks. The contribution expands fairness analysis to inequalities inside groups, while identifying and addressing a particular source of advantage for already connected nodes.
icml-2024-networked-inequality-preferent.tldr: The paper identifies within-group preferential attachment bias in a class of GCNs and proposes a fairness metric and mitigation strategy.

paragraphs: The linear ordering problem asks how to arrange a finite collection of elements when each ordered pair contributes a cost. The goal is an ordering with the smallest total cost. Because the problem is NP-hard and APX-hard, this paper investigates how to establish useful pieces of an optimal solution without first solving the entire ordering problem.

The authors introduce algorithms that efficiently determine, for some pairs, an ordering relationship that occurs in an optimal solution. They construct maps that transform one feasible ordering into another and derive conditions on the costs under which these maps are improving. Crucially, those conditions can be tested efficiently, making them usable as certificates for partial ordering decisions.

The contribution is partial optimality: fixing justified relationships while leaving the remaining order unresolved. A conclusion that a relationship occurs in an optimal solution does not assert that every optimum shares it. The authors evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of their conditions and algorithms on two datasets. This assesses how much useful structure the approach can recover and the computational effort required.
icml-2024-partial-optimality-in-the-line.tldr: Efficiently testable improvement conditions identify pairwise ordering decisions that belong to an optimal linear ordering.

paragraphs: Private everlasting prediction provides access to a prediction service without publicly releasing its learned hypothesis. The service labels an endless stream of examples drawn from the underlying distribution while protecting both the original training data and the incoming queries. This paper revises that framework and develops improved constructions within it.

One change incorporates robustness to poisoning attacks into the definition, making malicious interference part of the prediction problem. Another introduces a relaxed privacy definition suited to this setting. Under that definition, the privacy parameter delta can be disconnected from the total number of time steps. This distinction matters for a service intended to keep answering indefinitely, and the relaxation is part of the resulting claim.

The authors also provide new constructions for axis-aligned rectangles and decision stumps, reporting improvements in sample complexity and runtime over earlier work. These are specific prediction classes for which the framework receives concrete algorithms. The overall contribution combines a revised account of privacy and robustness with more efficient methods for maintaining a private prediction oracle over an unending query stream.
icml-2024-private-truly-everlasting-robu.tldr: The paper extends everlasting private prediction with poisoning robustness, a relaxed privacy definition, and more efficient constructions for two prediction classes.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning models can perform well in one environment yet struggle when that environment changes. Object-oriented methods offer a possible route to better transfer, but often require substantial domain knowledge or cover narrow settings. QORA learns an interpretable object-relational model directly from a domain-agnostic representation of states as objects.

The algorithm constructs models expressive enough to cover varied domains, including environments with stochastic transitions. The authors also introduce a benchmark suite for evaluating generalization. Their approach makes relationships and interactions among objects central to the learned model, and examples of its learned rules demonstrate that those rules are readily interpretable.

In the tested domains, QORA reaches 100% predictive accuracy with almost four orders of magnitude fewer observations than a neural-network baseline. It transfers to modified environments without additional training and adapts rapidly to tasks containing previously unseen object interactions. These are distinct capabilities: immediate transfer for the tested modifications and rapid learning for new interactions. The findings support the value of object-relational modeling within the evaluated domains.
icml-2024-qora-zero-shot-transfer-via-in.tldr: QORA learns interpretable object-relational models that achieve data-efficient prediction, zero-shot transfer, and rapid adaptation in its test domains.

paragraphs: Language models often generate programs individually, repeatedly rebuilding functionality that could be shared. ReGAL addresses this by learning a library of reusable functions from a small collection of existing programs. Its organizing idea is refactoring: restructuring code while preserving what its execution produces.

The method works without gradient-based learning and repeatedly checks and refines proposed abstractions through execution. The resulting library gives subsequent program generation reusable building blocks. The authors find that these functions capture both frequently repeated subroutines and environment dynamics, allowing learned abstractions to represent recurring behavior as well as common code fragments.

Across five datasets covering graphics, date reasoning, a text game, and mathematical tasks, both open-source and proprietary language models improve their program-prediction accuracy using ReGAL functions. For CodeLlama-13B, the reported absolute gains are 11.5 percentage points on LOGO, 26.1 on date understanding, and 8.1 on TextCraft, exceeding GPT-3.5 in two of those three domains. The results show that execution-checked reuse can make programs easier for models to predict across diverse evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-regal-refactoring-programs-to-.tldr: ReGAL refactors existing programs into execution-checked reusable libraries that improve language models’ program-generation accuracy.

paragraphs: Many material-design applications involve complex molecules assembled from known substructures, with relatively few examples available for learning. The paper argues that these settings have received less attention than small, drug-like molecules. It proposes a representation designed to make the available structural knowledge useful for both molecular generation and property prediction.

The method uses graph grammars to describe a hierarchical design space whose building blocks are molecular motifs. Molecules are represented through random walks over this space. This connects the representation to explicit construction rules, giving the model an interpretable account of molecular organization while supporting reasoning over complex structures.

The authors demonstrate advantages over existing methods in performance, efficiency, and the synthesizability of predicted molecules. They also provide detailed analysis of the method’s chemical interpretability. The contribution is a shared representation for proposing molecules and predicting their properties, grounded in the substructures used to design them. Its reported data efficiency is especially relevant to the motivating setting, where carefully designed molecules are complex and examples are scarce.
icml-2024-representing-molecules-as-rand.tldr: Random walks over interpretable molecular graph grammars support data-efficient molecule generation and property prediction.

paragraphs: The paper uses neural networks to investigate where the human brain may integrate visual and language information. It predicts stereoencephalography recordings collected while people watched movies. A site counts as evidence of integration when a multimodal model predicts its activity better than vision-only, language-only, or linearly combined vision-and-language models.

The authors first establish that trained visual and language models systematically predict these signals better than randomly initialized versions. They then compare models spanning different architectures and multimodal training methods. Because architecture, parameter count, and training data could complicate interpretation, they include a controlled comparison between SLIP and SimCLR that holds those attributes constant while changing input modality.

Using this approach, they identify an average of 141 out of 1,090 recording sites, or 12.94%, where multimodal integration appears to occur. Among the assessed training approaches, CLIP-style training best predicts activity at these sites. The findings locate candidate integration sites through comparative predictive performance; the evidence rests on that operational definition of integration and the accompanying controlled model comparison.
icml-2024-revealing-vision-language-inte.tldr: Comparing neural models’ predictions of brain recordings identifies candidate sites of vision-language integration during movie watching.

paragraphs: Verbal feedback offers a convenient way to customize a language model, but a contextual preference can spread too broadly. An instruction about tone in one kind of message may change behavior in unrelated situations. This paper finds that simply adding high-level feedback to a prompt can cause such overgeneralization.

The proposed method, Contextualized Critiques with Constrained Preference Optimization, or C3PO, turns feedback into a small synthetic preference dataset. The examples specify both how the preference should apply and where it should leave behavior unchanged. Fine-tuning then follows those preferences while minimizing divergence from the original model on prompts outside the feedback’s scope.

Experiments use high-level feedback written by humans and generated by GPT-4. C3PO follows the requested feedback comparably to in-context baselines while reducing overgeneralization by 30%. It also preserves behavior in unrelated contexts better than the compared methods. The contribution is a way to learn the boundary of a preference alongside the preference itself, making model customization more sensitive to the context in which a user intended it.
icml-2024-rlvf-learning-from-verbal-feed.tldr: C3PO learns contextual verbal preferences through synthetic examples and constrained fine-tuning, reducing reported overgeneralization by 30%.

paragraphs: Concept-based interpretability aims to explain a foundation model’s internal representations using high-level concepts. For those concepts to explain a complete example, they need to work together compositionally. This paper shows that existing unsupervised extraction methods produce concepts that lack that property, creating a gap between identifying concepts and explaining how they jointly account for a sample.

The authors identify two salient properties of compositional representations and introduce Compositional Concept Extraction, or CCE, to find concepts obeying them. The approach makes compositionality an explicit target of concept discovery. Its purpose is to produce a collection whose members combine meaningfully, so the explanation depends on how the concepts relate to the whole example.

Evaluation across five image and text datasets finds that CCE produces more compositional representations than the compared baselines. It also improves accuracy on four downstream classification tasks. These findings connect the explanatory goal to predictive usefulness: the extracted concepts better support joint descriptions of samples and provide representations that improve classification in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-towards-compositionality-in-co.tldr: CCE extracts concepts that combine more compositionally and improve downstream classification in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper addresses toxic language generation by intervening on a pretrained model’s internal neuron activations. The authors identify relevant neurons through their ability to distinguish toxic sentences. Their method, AUROC adaptation or AurA, reduces each neuron’s activation in proportion to that discriminative ability, avoiding model-dependent hyperparameters.

The reported evaluation finds toxicity reductions of up to 2.2 times with a perplexity increase of 0.72. Across tested models ranging from 1.5 billion to 40 billion parameters, AurA mitigates toxicity while preserving common-sense zero-shot abilities. These results assess both the desired behavioral change and the retention of useful capabilities across model scales.

AurA can also be combined with prompting strategies: the authors report that this increases its average mitigation potential from 1.28 times to 2.35 times. It additionally counters adversarial prompts intended to elicit toxic output. The contribution links a measurable property of individual neurons to a proportional intervention, offering an internal mechanism that can complement prompt-based approaches to toxicity reduction.
icml-2024-whispering-experts-neural-inte.tldr: AurA reduces toxic generation by proportionally suppressing neurons that distinguish toxic content, with benefits across the tested model scales.
